inferred_prompt: Describe what it would feel like to fall into a black hole, including sensations like weightlessness, crossing the event horizon, tidal forces, spaghettification, and the approach to the singularity.
style: general popular-science audience, vivid/evocative but factual tone

responses.text: Falling into a black hole would feel strangely uneventful at first: no jolt, no boundary, just silent, weightless drifting as you cross the event horizon without noticing. Around you, starlight would warp into shimmering rings, the universe compressing into a bright, distorted circle behind you. Then gravity's cruelty would emerge—your feet, closer to the center, pulled harder than your head, stretching you in a process physicists call spaghettification. For a supermassive black hole, this agony would be delayed, letting you glide deeper while time outside accelerated, distant stars flickering through eons. For a small one, you would be shredded instantly. Either way, the end is the singularity, where tidal forces grow infinite and sensation, along with you, simply ceases.

Falling into a black hole would be a terrifying and surreal experience beyond human comprehension. At first, you might feel weightless, drifting peacefully as spacetime curves around you. But as you approached the event horizon, tidal forces would begin stretching your body in a process scientists call "spaghettification," pulling you lengthwise while compressing you sideways. Time itself would warp — to an outside observer, you would appear to freeze at the horizon, yet from your perspective, you would plunge inward rapidly. Light would distort into bizarre patterns, and eventually every atom in your body would be torn apart completely.

Falling into a black hole would depend on its size, but for a large one, crossing the event horizon might feel unremarkable at first. As you plunged deeper, however, tidal forces would stretch your body vertically while compressing it horizontally, a gruesome process nicknamed "spaghettification." Time would warp strangely, and distant light might bend into surreal shapes. Eventually, the crushing gravity near the singularity would tear you apart atom by atom, ending your existence in unimaginable, inescapable darkness.
